components.note: 離 (traditional) — 隹 (bird) plus 离 as sound (lí). 离 was an old name for a mythical beast, so the 'leave' sense comes from 離; 离 kept only the sound part.
廾 (two hands) — in 開 two hands lift the bar of a gate; 开 is the simplified shape. Compare 关 (close).

example.english: He left Beijing yesterday.
example.fact: 离开 takes its object directly, with no preposition needed (离开北京, "to leave Beijing") — a common trap for English speakers who instinctively want to insert "from," since 离 alone already carries the sense of separation "away from" built into the verb itself.

examples.english: We leave the company at six.
He doesn't want to leave his family.

meanings: (used in negative expressions) (not) the least bit

components.note: 一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.
灬 (fire) — heat and burning, as in 热 hot, 照 shine, 黑 black; a dot is a small spot like a spark.
占 (zhàn) is a loose sound clue for diǎn; 占 also sounds out 站 zhàn and 粘 zhān.

example.english: I only understand a little Chinese.
example.fact: 一点 attached after a noun or adjective softens a statement into "a bit of X" (有一点贵, "a little expensive") — but the negative form 一点都不 intensifies rather than softens, flipping into "not in the least" (一点都不贵, "not expensive at all"), a construction that surprises learners expecting the negation to simply cancel the "a little" meaning.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng zài gěi wǒ yìdiǎn shuǐ.
examples.english: Please give me a little more water.

examples.pinyin: Jīntiān bù lěng, yìdiǎn yě bù lěng.
examples.english: It isn't cold today, not cold at all.

components.note: 一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.
宀 (roof) — houses and shelter, as in 家 home, 安 safe, 客 guest; settling down under a roof.
正 (zhèng, upright; the lower part is written 疋) is a loose sound clue for dìng; also in 证 zhèng and 政 zhèng.

example.english: You must definitely come tomorrow.
example.fact: 一定 sits near the top of Mandarin’s certainty ladder alongside 肯定 (also in this batch) — but 一定 leans toward expressing a strong intention or requirement ("一定要," "must"), while 肯定 leans toward a confident assessment of fact ("肯定是," "it’s definitely [true that]"), a nuance easy to blur since English "definitely" covers both.

examples.english: I'll definitely come.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yídìng hěn lèi le ba?
examples.english: You must be very tired, right?

components.note: 走 (walk, run) — movement, as in 赶 chase, 超 surpass, 越 cross over; 起 is to rise or get up.
己 (jǐ) is a loose sound clue for qǐ; 己 also sounds out 记 jì and 纪 jì.

example.english: I get up at six every day.
example.fact: 起 works as a verb and a direction ending: 起床 'get up', 站起来 'stand up', 想起来 'remember'. It also forms 一起 'together' and 对不起 'sorry'. 起 counts incidents in speech: 一起事故.

examples.english: What time do you get up?
Sorry, I'm late.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement, as in 过, 近, 送: 还 is to go back or return (huán), then "still" (hái).
不 here stands in for 睘 (huán) in the traditional 還, so it is not a real clue; same stand-in in 环 huán.
日 (sun) — on top; the usual explanation is sun over 正 "straight, correct": what is clear and straight is "right, is". A memory aid, not firm etymology.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào hē chá háishi kāfēi?
example.english: Do you want to drink tea or coffee?
example.fact: 还是 does double duty as both "still" (还是老样子, "still the same as before") and the choice-question connector "or" (茶还是咖啡, "tea or coffee") — two meanings that look unrelated in English but share an underlying sense of "as before, among the alternatives already on the table."

examples.english: Do you like red or blue?

examples.hanzi: 已经十点了,他还是没回来。
examples.pinyin: Yǐjīng shí diǎn le, tā háishi méi huílái.
examples.english: It's already ten o'clock and he still hasn't come back.

components.note: 发 (send out, hair) — two characters merged in simplified writing: 發 fā "emit, issue" and 髮 fà "hair" (头发).
王 (jade) — on the left, 王 is the jade radical, as in 球 ball, 玩 play, 理 reason; jade is bright and shows itself.
见 (jiàn, see) is a close sound clue (xiàn) and also fits the meaning: appear so it can be seen.

example.hanzi: 科学家发现了一种新的病毒。
example.pinyin: Kēxuéjiā fāxiàn le yì zhǒng xīn de bìngdú.
example.english: Scientists discovered a new virus.
example.fact: 发现 combines 发 ("to bring forth") with 现, built from 见 ("to see") — literally "to bring into sight," a vivid image for discovery. It shares its first character with 发生 (also in this batch, "to happen"), two related but distinct extensions of 发’s core sense "to emit, set forth."

examples.pinyin: Wǒ fāxiàn qiánbāo bú jiàn le.
examples.english: I discovered my wallet was missing.
She realized she was wrong.

components.note: 斤 (axe) — cutting tools, as in 新 new and 斩 chop. 所 once echoed the sound of chopping; "place" and "that which" are later borrowed uses.

example.english: This school is very big.
example.fact: 所 is a measure word for institutions (一所大学). It also appears in 所以 'therefore', 所有 'all', and the pattern 因为…所以… 'because…so…'. In formal writing it turns verbs into nouns: 所见 'what one sees'.

examples.pinyin: Tāmen zài yì suǒ dàxué gōngzuò.
examples.english: They work at a university.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiù shì wǒ suǒ shuō de wèntí.
examples.english: This is the problem I was talking about.

components.note: 亻 (person) — people, as in 你, 他, 做.
主 (zhǔ) is a close sound clue for zhù; also in 注 zhù and 柱 zhù, and 主 means master (a person who stays).

example.english: I live in Beijing.
example.fact: 住 is 'to reside' and 'to stay overnight': 住酒店 'stay at a hotel'. As a verb ending it means 'firmly': 记住 'remember', 站住 'halt!', 拿住 'hold on'. 住院 means 'be hospitalised'.

examples.english: Which floor do you live on?
Please hold on to this bag.

components.note: 亻 (person radical, 单人旁) — people and what they do: 你, 他, 位.
牛 (ox) — in the traditional reading, a person 亻 dividing up an ox: one piece, hence 件 as a measure word for items.

example.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le yí jiàn yīfu.
example.english: I bought a piece of clothing.
example.fact: 件 counts upper-body clothing (一件衬衫), matters (一件事), and documents or luggage (一件行李). For trousers or skirts the measure word is 条. 件 also appears in 文件 'document' and 邮件 'mail'.

examples.english: How much is this piece of clothing?

examples.pinyin: Jīntiān yǒu liǎng jiàn zhòngyào de shì.
examples.english: There are two important things today.

components.note: 止 (foot) — a foot heading straight for a target line: upright, correct. 正 gives sound to 证 zhèng, 整 zhěng and 政 zhèng.

example.english: He is reading right now.
example.fact: 正在 + verb shows an action in progress. 正 also means 'exactly': 正好 'just right', 正确 'correct'. When it means 'first month', 正月, it is read zhēng.

examples.english: It's pouring rain right now.
We're in a meeting, please wait a moment.

components.note: 而 (and, but) — oldest form is a beard (compare 须 xū, beard), later borrowed for the conjunction; 而 survives in 耐 nài.
且 (moreover) — an old picture of an offering stand or ancestral tablet. As a sound clue it gives 祖 zǔ, 组 zǔ, 租 zū and 助 zhù.

example.hanzi: 这家餐厅很便宜,而且很好吃。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā cāntīng hěn piányi, érqiě hěn hǎochī.
example.english: This restaurant is cheap, and moreover it's delicious.
example.fact: 而且 typically completes a "不但...而且..." ("not only...but also...") frame when both halves of a sentence are explicitly marked, though in casual speech 不但 is often dropped while 而且 alone still carries the "and what’s more" sense on its own.

examples.hanzi: 他会说英语,而且说得很好。
examples.pinyin: Tā huì shuō Yīngyǔ, érqiě shuō de hěn hǎo.
examples.english: He can speak English, and speaks it very well.

examples.pinyin: Jīntiān hěn lěng, érqiě xiàzhe yǔ.
examples.english: It's cold today, and it's raining too.

components.note: 并 (combine) — simplified from 並, which showed two figures standing side by side; hence together, also, and (并且).

example.pinyin: Wǒ bìng bù zhīdào zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: I really don't know about this matter.
example.fact: 并 before 不 or 没 strengthens a denial: 并不贵 'not expensive at all'. 并且 means 'moreover'. Its basic sense 'side by side' appears in 并排 'side by side' and 合并 'merge'.

examples.english: I'm actually not angry.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shìqing bìng bú tài nán.
examples.english: This matter isn't that hard.

components.note: 必 (bì) is a sound clue for 秘 mì, 密 mì and 蜜 mì: the same series, with only the initial changing.
页 (head) — heads and faces, as in 头 head, 顶 top, 题 title.
彡 (hair strokes) — hair or beard on the face, as in 影 shadow; together a beard, later "must" (必须).

example.english: You must finish your homework first.
example.fact: 必须 marks a hard, often external obligation — a rule or requirement that isn’t optional — sitting at the strongest end of the want/need/must spectrum the pilot batch’s 需要 entry (rank 28) lays out, stronger than both 要 ("want") and 需要 ("need").

examples.english: You must bring your ID.
You must get up early tomorrow.

components.note: 心 (heart) — mind and feelings, as in 想, 思, 感: 意 is what one has in mind.
音 (yīn, sound) is a loose sound clue for yì; 意 itself gives 忆 yì and 亿 yì.
田 here replaces 囟 (skull) in the older form: head over heart
心 (heart) — thinking and feeling, as in 想, 意, 感: 思 is to think over, with head and heart.

example.english: What does this word mean?
example.fact: 意思 anchors two fixed phrases that both trip up learners: 有意思 means "interesting" (literally "has meaning/interest"), while 不好意思 means "excuse me, embarrassed" (literally "not good meaning") — neither English translation obviously has anything to do with "meaning," despite both being built directly from 意思.

examples.pinyin: Tā de huà shì shénme yìsi?
examples.english: What does he mean?

examples.pinyin: Zhè běn shū hěn yǒu yìsi.
examples.english: This book is very interesting.

components.note: 攵 (tap, strike) — hand with stick, as in 教, 收, 改: to drive away, set free.
方 (fāng) is a close sound clue for fàng; 方 also in 房 fáng and 访 fǎng.

example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ shū fàng zài zhuōzi shàng.
example.english: Please put the book on the table.
example.fact: 放 means to place something or to release it: 放心 'rest assured', 放假 'have a holiday', 放学 'school lets out'. It also means 'play (a recording)': 放音乐.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ bǎ shǒujī fàng zài nǎr le?
examples.english: Where did you put your phone?
We have a holiday this weekend.

components.note: 一 (line) — dictionary reads 不 as a bird flying up toward the sky 一. The meaning 'not' is a borrowing, so the shape does not explain it today.
杯 (bēi) — a character that uses 不 as a loose sound clue (木 + 不). The sound is a hint only: 不 bù vs bēi.
钅 (metal, simplified 金) — metals, as in 钱 money, 铁 iron, 铜 copper; 错 first meant to inlay metal.
昔 (xī) is a loose sound clue for cuò; 昔 also sounds out 借 jiè, 措 cuò and 惜 xī.

example.english: This idea is not bad.
example.fact: 不错 literally negates 错 ("mistake, wrong") to get "not wrong" — but in everyday use it has drifted from a neutral "correct" into a mild positive compliment, "pretty good," the same kind of understated-praise shift English speakers make when they say something is "not bad" and mean it as a genuine compliment.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ de Zhōngwén shuō de bú cuò.
examples.english: Your Chinese is pretty good.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiā fànguǎn de cài bú cuò.
examples.english: The food at this restaurant is not bad.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — the bottom part, the meat/body radical as in 脑, 脚, 胖. Early forms show meat on a bone, but that does not explain 'willing' today.
止 (stop, foot) — the top. Dictionary story: stop 止 flexing muscle ⺼. Memory aid: you stop resisting and agree — 肯定, a hedged mnemonic.
宀 (roof) — houses and shelter, as in 家 home, 安 safe, 客 guest; settling down under a roof.
正 (zhèng, upright; the lower part is written 疋) is a loose sound clue for dìng; also in 证 zhèng and 政 zhèng.

example.pinyin: Tā kěndìng zhīdào zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He definitely knows about this matter.
example.fact: 肯定 can double as a verb meaning "to affirm, to give recognition to" (肯定他的努力, "to acknowledge his effort") on top of its more common adverbial sense "definitely, for sure" — two senses that share the same core idea of affirming something as real or worthy, whether that something is a fact or a person’s effort.

examples.english: I'm sure he'll agree.
The teacher affirmed my idea.

components.note: 电 (electric) — simplified from 電: 雨 rain over 申, a lightning bolt (申 originally pictured a flash).
讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 说, 请, 谢; 话 is speech.
舌 (shé, tongue) fits the meaning (speaking) and is a loose sound clue for huà; also in 活 huó.

example.english: I'll call you.
example.fact: 电话 combines 电 ("electricity" — itself a simplified pictograph of a lightning bolt, per this word’s own character notes) with 话 ("speech, words") into a strikingly literal "electric speech," a compound coined when the telephone was still a genuinely new technology needing a brand-new word.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ de diànhuà hàomǎ shì duōshao?
examples.english: What's your phone number?
He's answering the phone.

components.note: 力 (strength) — visible inside 为. Memory aid: putting strength 力 into doing something; 为 is 'to do, to act' and, in 因为, 为什么, 'because/for'.
為 (traditional) — often explained as a hand leading an elephant to work. 为 is a cursive simplification, so the picture is no longer visible.
子 (child) — 了 is usually read as a swaddled baby, like 子 without the arms. Its meanings 'finish' (了解 liǎo) and the particle le were borrowed later.

example.hanzi: 为了健康,他每天都运动。
example.pinyin: Wèile jiànkāng, tā měitiān dōu yùndòng.
example.english: For the sake of his health, he exercises every day.
example.fact: 为了 typically opens a sentence to state a goal before the main clause describes the action taken to reach it ("为了 + goal, + action") — roughly the mirror image of English, which usually states the action first and tacks the purpose on afterward with "in order to" or "so that."

examples.hanzi: 为了你,我什么都愿意做。
examples.pinyin: Wèile nǐ, wǒ shénme dōu yuànyì zuò.
examples.english: I'd do anything for you.

examples.hanzi: 他为了赶火车,跑得很快。
examples.pinyin: Tā wèile gǎn huǒchē, pǎo de hěn kuài.
examples.english: He ran fast in order to catch the train.

components.note: 扌 (hand, 提手旁) — marks hand actions, as in 打 hit, 推 push; 搞 is a flexible verb for doing or handling something.
高 (gāo) — close sound: 搞 gǎo. 高 also sounds out 稿 gǎo and 糕 gāo.

example.english: What are you up to?
example.fact: 搞 is a colloquial catch-all verb: 搞定 'get it done', 搞错 'get it wrong', 搞笑 'funny'. It can sound slightly informal, even negative (搞鬼 'play tricks'), so it isn't used in formal writing.

examples.english: He got the time wrong.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì wǒ lái gǎodìng.
examples.english: I'll take care of this.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 木 is wood, as in 桌, 板, 树; 棒 is a stick.
奉 (fèng) — loose hint — 棒 is bàng; 奉 also sounds out 捧 pěng.

example.english: Your Chinese is great!
example.fact: 棒 literally means 'stick' (棒球 'baseball'), but in speech it's a casual 'great': 真棒！ 'Awesome!' 你真棒 is a popular praise for children and learners.

examples.english: This idea is great!

examples.pinyin: Tā de lánqiú dǎ de hěn bàng.
examples.english: He plays basketball really well.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — bamboo slips, once used for writing and lists, as in 等 wait, 笔 pen, 笑 laugh.
弟 (dì) gives the exact sound; 弟 also sounds out 梯 tī and 剃 tì.
一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ dìyī cì lái Zhōngguó.
example.english: This is my first time coming to China.
example.fact: 第 attaches to a number to form an ordinal — pictured, per this word’s own character notes, as bamboo strips (⺮) once used for writing, sorted into sequential order — so 第一 literally frames "first" as "the first [strip] in the sorted stack," the same 第 that marks every ordinal in Chinese (第二, 第三, and so on).

examples.pinyin: Tā shì wǒmen bān dì yī míng.
examples.english: She's first in our class.

examples.hanzi: 你第一天上班感觉怎么样?
examples.pinyin: Nǐ dì yī tiān shàngbān gǎnjué zěnmeyàng?
examples.english: How did you feel on your first day of work?

components.note: 女 (woman) — women and family, as in 她, 姐, 奶; 妈 is mother.
马 (mǎ) is a close sound clue for mā; also in 吗 ma, 骂 mà and 码 mǎ.

example.english: Mom, I'm home.
example.fact: 妈 is usually doubled to 妈妈. A classic tone-practice sentence is 妈妈骂马 'Mom scolds the horse' (Māma mà mǎ), which combines 妈, 骂 and 马.

examples.english: Mom, what's for dinner?
My parents live in Shanghai.

components.note: 土 (earth) — ground and place, as in 场 field, 城 city, 坐 sit.
也 (yě) is a loose sound clue for dì; 也 also sounds out 他 tā and 池 chí.

example.english: He is sitting on the ground.
example.fact: 地 dì is 'ground' and 'place': 地方 'place', 地铁 'subway', 土地 'land'. The same character is also the structural particle de that turns adjectives into adverbs: 慢慢地走 'walk slowly'.

examples.english: Where shall we go to eat?
He walked slowly into the room.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement, as in 过, 近, 送: to go forward.
井 stands in for 隹 of 進, a loose clue only.

example.english: Please come in and sit.
example.fact: 进 is 'enter', the opposite of 出. It shows direction after verbs: 走进来 'walk in'. It also means 'to advance': 进步 'progress'. 进口 means both 'entrance' and 'import'.

examples.english: Come in, the door isn't locked.
He walked into the classroom.

components.note: 阝 on the right is 邑 (city) — places, as in 都 capital, 邮 post, 部 part. 那 was a place name before it meant "that".
木 (tree) — wood, as in 桌 table, 板 board; 样 once meant a tree (acorn) and later "form, pattern".
羊 (yáng, sheep) is a near-exact sound clue for yàng; 羊 also sounds out 洋 yáng and 养 yǎng.

example.english: Don't talk like that, the way he does.
example.fact: 那样 mirrors the pilot batch’s 这样 (rank 13) exactly, with the far-demonstrative 那 swapped in for the near 这, and inherits the same manner-vs-degree contrast that entry describes: 那样 describes how something is done, while 那么 (pilot batch, rank 30) more often modifies degree before an adjective.

examples.english: I don't want to do it that way.
That's just the kind of person he is.

components.note: 大 (big) — a front-facing person with arms and legs spread wide: big. As radical, 大 is in 天 sky, 太 too much, 夫 man.
宀 (roof) — houses and shelter, as in 室 room, 安 safe, 字 character; 家 is home.
豕 (pig) — a pig under a roof: pigs were kept in the home, hence home and family.

example.pinyin: Dàjiā hǎo, wǒ jiào Xiǎo Lǐ.
example.english: Hello everyone, my name is Xiao Li.
example.fact: 大家 combines 大 ("big") with 家 ("family, household") into an old image of one big, extended "family" encompassing everyone present. 家’s own character notes trace it to 宀 (a roof) over 豕 (a pig, once a practical marker of a household) — so 大家 quietly carries a household metaphor into its modern, completely general sense of "everyone."

examples.english: Has everyone arrived?
This is everyone's opinion.

components.note: 斤 (axe) — chopping, as in 所, 斩: freshly cut wood is new (薪 xīn is firewood).
亲 (qīn) is a close sound clue for xīn.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yí ge xīn shǒujī.
example.english: I have a new phone.
example.fact: 新 appears in 新年 'New Year', 新闻 'news', 新鲜 'fresh'. Its opposite is 旧. As an adverb it means 'newly': 新来的 'newly arrived'. 新 is also the first part of the country name 新加坡 'Singapore'.

examples.english: The New Year is coming soon.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen yǒu yí wèi xīn tóngshì.
examples.english: We have a new colleague.

components.note: 你 (nǐ, you) — the base word; adding 心 makes it the polite form.
心 (heart) — respect from the heart; also in 想 think, 爱 love.

example.english: Please have a seat.
example.fact: 您 is the respectful 'you' for elders, customers or strangers. It is singular, so for two people say 您二位 rather than 您们. Using 您 with friends sounds distant or jokingly formal.

examples.english: May I ask your surname?
Thank you for your help.

components.note: 向 (toward) — a window 口 in a wall facing a direction, hence toward. It also gives its sound to 响 xiǎng and 饷 xiǎng.

example.english: Please walk to the left.
example.fact: 向 as a preposition means 'towards': 向前看 'look ahead', 向他道歉 'apologise to him', 向老师学习 'learn from the teacher'. 方向 means 'direction', and 一向 means 'all along'.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng xiàng qián zǒu, ránhòu xiàng yòu guǎi.
examples.english: Please walk straight ahead, then turn right.
I want to learn from you.

components.note: 一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.
此 (cǐ) is a loose sound clue for xiē; 此 also sounds out 紫 zǐ and 雌 cí. 些 is the plural-ish "some, a few".

example.english: I bought some fruit.
example.fact: 一些 is built the same way as the pilot batch’s 这些 and this batch’s own 那些 — a demonstrative fused with 些, Mandarin’s built-in small-plural marker — except 一些 drops the demonstrative entirely, using bare "one" to mean an unspecified small quantity rather than pointing at a specific group.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng wèn nǐ yìxiē wèntí.
examples.english: I'd like to ask you a few questions.
Give him some time.

components.note: 三 — three strokes, one more than 二. The numbers 一 二 三 are the only ones counted by drawing lines.

example.english: I have three friends.
example.fact: 三 is also written 叁 on contracts and cheques, where the extra strokes make forgery harder. It can mean 'several' in idioms: 三思 'think carefully', 再三 'repeatedly'. 三月 is March.

examples.english: It's half past three now.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen jiā yǒu sān kǒu rén.
examples.english: There are three people in my family.

components.note: 阝 on the right is 邑 (city) — places, as in 都 capital, 邮 post, 部 part. 那 was a place name before it meant "that".
田 (field) — farmland, the village's fields.
土 (earth) — land; field + earth gives "village" and then the unit of distance. 里 is the sound part of 理 lǐ.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen bǎ chē tíng zài nàli.
example.english: We parked the car over there.
example.fact: 那里 pairs with the pilot batch’s 这里 (rank 17) as Mandarin’s standard far/near "there"/"here," and like 这里, it has its own casual, erhua-suffixed cousin — 那儿, alongside 这儿 (also in this batch) — giving both demonstratives parallel formal and colloquial forms.

examples.pinyin: Tā zài nàlǐ gōngzuòle wǔ nián.
examples.english: He has worked there for five years.
What's the weather like there?

components.note: 人 (person) — the right-hand part. The left part is a hook-and-dot, from an old tool-like shape. Meaning 'by means of, so as to' is not shown by the parts today.
Memory aid: a person 人 using a tool to get something done — 'by means of' (可以, 所以, 以前). A mnemonic, not proven etymology.
力 (strength) — visible inside 为. Memory aid: putting strength 力 into doing something; 为 is 'to do, to act' and, in 因为, 为什么, 'because/for'.
為 (traditional) — often explained as a hand leading an elephant to work. 为 is a cursive simplification, so the picture is no longer visible.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǐwéi nǐ yǐjīng zǒu le.
example.english: I thought you had already left.
example.fact: 以为 carries a strong implication that the belief turned out to be mistaken — 我以为你走了 implies the speaker has just discovered they were wrong — unlike the neutral 认为 (also in this batch) or 觉得 (pilot batch, rank 23), which carry no built-in suggestion of error.

examples.english: I thought today was Friday.

examples.pinyin: Tā yǐwéi wǒ bú huì zuòfàn.
examples.english: He thought I couldn't cook.

components.note: 高 (tall) — a drawing of a tall tower building. 高 also sounds out 糕 gāo (cake), 搞 gǎo and 稿 gǎo.
興 (traditional) — several hands lifting together, so to raise, stir, flourish. 兴 keeps only a few strokes; 高兴 is 'high spirits' and 兴趣 is 'interest'.

example.english: I'm very happy to meet you.
example.fact: 高兴 typically names an immediate, situational happiness triggered by a specific event ("很高兴认识你," "happy to meet you"), while 开心 and 快乐 lean toward a more general, ongoing good mood or well-wish (as in 生日快乐, "happy birthday") — a distinction English’s all-purpose "happy" doesn’t force speakers to make.

examples.english: I'm very happy today.
He jumped up happily.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — marks speech, sounds and eating, as in 叫 call, 吃 eat, 唱 sing; 嘛 is a particle added to a sentence for emphasis or persuasion.
麻 (má) — same sound: 嘛 má. 麻 also sounds out 吗 ma, the question particle.

example.english: It's simple, you see.
example.fact: 嘛 ends a sentence to say 'it's obvious' or to coax: 不会就问嘛 'just ask if you don't know'. It is warmer or more insistent than 吗, and it is toneless here.

examples.english: Just try it yourself.

examples.pinyin: Bú huì jiù xué ma, méi guānxi.
examples.english: If you can't, just learn, it's fine.

components.note: 耂 (old) — 老 pictures an old person with long hair leaning on a staff; the short form 耂 is also in 考 test and 孝 filial.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ de lǎo péngyou.
example.english: He is my old friend.
example.fact: 老 is respectful in Chinese: 老师 'teacher', 老板 'boss', 老人 'elder'. It also means 'always' (老是迟到 'always late') and prefixes names: 老王. 老 for friends means long-standing, not elderly.

examples.english: The teacher explained it very clearly.
He is always forgetting to bring his keys.

components.note: 亻 (person radical, 单人旁) — people and what they do: 你, 他, 住.
立 (stand) — the spot where a person 亻 stands 立: a position or seat; also 位置 position.

example.english: How many in your party?
example.fact: 位 is the polite measure word for people: 三位客人 'three guests'. As a noun it means 'position': 座位 'seat', 位置 'location', 学位 'degree'. In restaurants 几位？ is the standard question to guests.

examples.english: How many in your party, please?

examples.pinyin: Zhè wèi shì wǒ de tóngshì.
examples.english: This is my colleague.

meanings: to be able to take care of

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement, as in 这, 近, 送: 过 is to pass or cross.
寸 here replaces 咼 (guō) of the traditional 過, so it is not a sound clue; 咼 survives in 锅 guō and 祸 huò.
来 (come) — it began as a picture of a wheat plant; the sound was borrowed for "come". 麦 (wheat) still shows it, with a root 夂 added.

example.pinyin: Nǐ néng guòlái bāng wǒ yíxià ma?
example.english: Can you come over and help me for a bit?
example.fact: 过来 completes a trio of "toward the speaker" directional verbs alongside 回来 and 出来 (both also in this batch) — 过 alone contributes "passing across, crossing over," so 过来 pictures someone crossing some distance to arrive at the speaker’s side, while swapping in 去 for 过去 sends them crossing away instead.

examples.english: Please come over and take a look.

examples.pinyin: Tā cóng nàbian zǒu guòlái le.
examples.english: He walked over from that side.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — hand radical for actions — 掉 is to drop or lose hold.

example.english: My phone fell.
example.fact: 掉 is 'fall' and also a verb ending of removal: 吃掉 'eat up', 扔掉 'throw away', 丢掉 'lose'. 掉头 means 'turn around' (a vehicle).

examples.english: The cup fell on the floor.

examples.hanzi: 你把这些旧报纸扔掉吧。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ bǎ zhèxiē jiù bàozhǐ rēngdiào ba.
examples.english: Throw away these old newspapers.

components.note: 儿 (legs, person) — with a foot 𠂉 above: a foot stepping out in front of a person, so "first, earlier".

example.english: You go first.
example.fact: 先 is 'first': 先…再… 'first…then…' sequences actions. 先生 literally means 'one born earlier' and is used for 'Mr.', 'teacher' and 'husband'. 先 comes before the verb.

examples.english: Sit down for a while first.
Sir, what would you like to order?

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — bamboo slips arranged in an even row; 等 means "rank, equal" and then "wait".
寺 (sì) is only a loose sound clue for děng; 寺 also in 诗 shī and 持 chí.
⺮ (bamboo) — bamboo slips arranged in an even row; 等 means "rank, equal" and then "wait".
寺 (sì) is only a loose sound clue for děng; 寺 also in 诗 shī and 持 chí.

example.hanzi: 桌子上有苹果、香蕉等等。
example.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng yǒu píngguǒ, xiāngjiāo děngděng.
example.english: There are apples, bananas, etc. on the table.
example.fact: 等等 is one word doing two unrelated jobs depending on context: reduplicated at the end of a list it trails off into "etcetera," but called out on its own as an interjection it means "wait!, hold on!" — the same character 等 ("to wait") underlies both, just put to very different use in each role.

examples.english: I like apples, pears, and so on.
Wait, I haven't finished yet.

components.note: 土 (earth) — a green shoot pushing up from the ground: growth, birth, life. 生 also sounds out 性 xìng, 姓 xìng and 星 xīng.
氵 (water) — water and liquids, as in 河, 海, 汤; water means life: 活 is alive.
舌 (shé, tongue) is a loose sound clue for huó; also in 话 huà.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xǐhuan xiànzài de shēnghuó.
example.english: I really like my life right now.
example.fact: 生活 refers to everyday living or lifestyle — how one spends one's days — and is a common false-friend trap for learners who reach for it to translate “life” in the biological sense; that meaning instead belongs to 生命, as in 生命危险 (“life-threatening danger”), never 生活危险.

examples.english: A student's life is busy.

examples.hanzi: 他在农村生活了二十年。
examples.pinyin: Tā zài nóngcūn shēnghuóle èrshí nián.
examples.english: He lived in the countryside for twenty years.

components.note: 之 (of, go) — oldest form is a foot leaving a starting line: "to go". Now it is a literary particle meaning "of" or "it".

example.pinyin: Chī fàn zhīqián qǐng xǐ shǒu.
example.english: Please wash your hands before eating.
example.fact: 之 is the classical 'of' (的) that survives in set phrases: 之前 'before', 之后 'after', 之间 'between'. Fractions use it: 三分之一 'one third', 百分之十 'ten percent'.

examples.pinyin: Sān fēn zhī yī de rén méiyǒu lái.
examples.english: One third of the people didn't come.
Please turn off the lights before you go out.

components.note: 买 (simplified 買) — the old form shows a net 网 over a shell 贝 (money): netting goods, to buy. 卖 mài sell is built on 买.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng mǎi yì bēi kāfēi.
example.english: I'd like to buy a coffee.
example.fact: 买 (mǎi) and 卖 (mài) look alike; 卖 has an extra 十 on top, and a handy rule is that 'selling' has more on top. Together they make 买卖 'business'. 买单 is 'ask for the bill', a common phrase in restaurants.

examples.english: I'm going to the supermarket to buy milk.
Did you manage to get the tickets?

components.note: 禾 (grain) — crops, as in 秋 autumn, 租 rent, 和 and 秒 second; 种 is seed or to plant.
中 (zhōng) is a close sound clue for zhǒng/zhòng.

example.english: This kind of fruit is very sweet.
example.fact: 种 zhǒng is 'kind' as a measure word (这种, 各种 'all kinds') and 'seed'. Read zhòng it means 'to plant': 种花 'grow flowers'. The tones separate the two uses.

examples.english: Which kind of color do you like?

examples.pinyin: Yéye zài yuànzi lǐ zhòng huā.
examples.english: Grandpa is growing flowers in the yard.

components.note: 医 (doctor) — simplified from 醫, which had 酉 (medicinal wine, as in 酒) at the bottom; the box 匚 and arrow 矢 remain.
土 (earth) — a green shoot pushing up from the ground: growth, birth, life. 生 also sounds out 性 xìng, 姓 xìng and 星 xīng.

example.pinyin: Yīshēng shuō wǒ xūyào duō xiūxi.
example.english: The doctor said I need to rest more.
example.fact: 医 already meant “to cure” on its own (built from 矢, arrow — treating arrow wounds was one of medicine's earliest jobs) — 医生 literally reads as “one who cures the living,” pairing that cure-verb with 生 (“to live, life”).

examples.english: I'm going to see a doctor.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de jiějie shì yì míng yīshēng.
examples.english: My older sister is a doctor.

components.note: 取 (qǔ, take) is the base; the loose sound clue also appears in 趣 qù and 娶 qǔ. The top 日 here is an old cap shape, not the sun.
后 (after, behind) — two words merged in simplified writing: old 后 "ruler" (皇后 empress) and 後 "behind, later" (as in 然后).

example.pinyin: Zuìhòu, tā juédìng liú zài Běijīng.
example.english: In the end, he decided to stay in Beijing.
example.fact: 最后 typically opens a sentence as a transitional adverb (“finally, in the end”) summarizing a sequence, while directly before another noun (最后一天, “the last day”) it functions more like an ordinary adjective — one word covering both an English adverb and an adjective.

examples.hanzi: 最后一班车已经开走了。
examples.pinyin: Zuìhòu yì bān chē yǐjīng kāizǒu le.
examples.english: The last bus has already left.

examples.hanzi: 你最后一次见他是什么时候?
examples.pinyin: Nǐ zuìhòu yí cì jiàn tā shì shénme shíhou?
examples.english: When was the last time you saw him?

components.note: 之 (of, go) — oldest form is a foot leaving a starting line: "to go". Now it is a literary particle meaning "of" or "it".
刂 (knife) — the right-hand side. Usually about cutting (到, 别, 利), but not in 前: it is a later corruption of the old picture.
舟 (boat) — hidden in the old form: a foot on a boat moving ahead, so 'in front, forward'. Usual explanation, though the modern shape hides it.

example.pinyin: Shuìjiào zhīqián, wǒ xǐhuan kàn shū.
example.english: Before going to sleep, I like to read.
example.fact: 之前 almost always follows the event it's relative to, rather than preceding it the way English “before” does — Chinese says literally “sleep-before” (睡觉之前) where English says “before sleep,” a mirrored word order that trips up many learners building their first time clauses.

examples.pinyin: Chīfàn zhīqián yào xiān xǐ shǒu.
examples.english: Wash your hands before eating.

examples.hanzi: 三年之前,我还不会说中文。
examples.pinyin: Sān nián zhīqián, wǒ hái bú huì shuō Zhōngwén.
examples.english: Three years ago, I couldn't speak Chinese yet.

components.note: 亻 (person) — people, as in 你, 他, 们: 伙 is a companion.
火 (huǒ, fire) gives the exact sound; 火 also means fire.
讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 说, 请, 谢; counting aloud.
十 (ten) — counting up to ten: 计 is to count and reckon.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ zuì hǎo de huǒji.
example.english: He's my best partner.
example.fact: 伙计 combines 伙 (“companion, mate” — people who share meals or work together) with 计 (“to reckon, to plan”) — originally a business partner one “reckoned accounts” with, the word later slid down in register to also mean an ordinary shop hand or waiter.

examples.pinyin: Hēi, huǒji, nǐ zài gàn shénme?
examples.english: Hey buddy, what are you up to?
This fellow works very conscientiously.
